stem: A nurse sustains an occupational blood exposure. After immediate first aid to the exposed site, what should the nurse do next?

options.A: Report the exposure immediately and seek medical evaluation
options.B: Wait to report the exposure unless symptoms of infection develop
options.C: Document the exposure at the end of the month if no symptoms occur
options.D: Continue working without reporting because post-exposure assessment is optional

rationale: Current CDC/NIOSH guidance instructs healthcare workers to report blood and body-fluid exposures immediately and to seek medical care promptly so the exposure risk can be assessed and post-exposure management provided when indicated. Waiting for symptoms or delaying reporting can postpone time-sensitive evaluation and prophylaxis. Therefore A is the best action.
educational_objective: Report occupational blood or body-fluid exposures immediately and obtain prompt medical evaluation after initial first aid.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
source_document_title: Bloodborne Infectious Disease Risk Factors — Healthcare Workers
source_locator: Treatment: provide immediate care after exposure, report the incident to your supervisor, immediately seek medical care to determine risk; Prevention — Reporting: report blood and body-fluid exposure immediately
source_claim_supported: After an occupational blood/body-fluid exposure, healthcare workers should report the incident immediately and seek prompt medical evaluation after initial first aid.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: follow exposure-control and infection-prevention procedures after occupational exposure
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — occupational bloodborne-pathogen exposure response
correction_summary: Removed the vague 'as soon as possible per facility protocol' phrasing and anchored the item to current CDC/NIOSH wording: report immediately and seek medical evaluation promptly. Avoided importing a specific HIV PEP timing threshold into a generic bloodborne-exposure item.
audit_findings: A exactly reflects current CDC/NIOSH guidance. B and C improperly delay reporting; D falsely makes exposure assessment optional. The item is generic to occupational blood exposure and therefore does not overstate pathogen-specific prophylaxis rules. No second answer, cueing, or unsupported timing precision remains.
